text: I will test the proposed market transplant against the actual mechanisms and confounds in both papers. Initial focus: whether P supplies real endogenous stakes or instead changes the objective and measurement enough that Q’s allocative-efficiency result is no longer comparable; I will seek a sharper mechanism-level intervention if so.

I will test the proposed transplant against the papers actual causal structures. Initial alternative: use P energy accounting to endogenize Q time/compute costs and distinguish impatience from survival pressure, with preregistered crossed treatments rather than merely embedding a generic auction. I will inspect whether P has a scarce allocation mechanism suitable for auctioning and whether Q urgency evidence is causal or only lexical association.

I am changing the proposed connection. A full double-auction transplant into P's job loop confounds institution, task, models, and incentives. The sharper joint experiment keeps Q's Smith market fixed and imports only P's endogenous inference-cost budget: debit each agent by \(C=kT S^{\alpha}\) for every market call, with deactivation or a finite decision budget. Q identifies penny-incrementing and reluctance to cross as the proximal cause of low volume (Q, lines 319--348) but its urgency lexicon is correlational and explicitly does not establish what causes switching (Q, lines 405--435). P supplies a manipulable cost on reasoning and evidence that token-cost pressure changes participation/efficiency (P, lines 147--205, 298--324). Core causal question: does pricing deliberation eliminate strategic dawdling and improve surplus, or merely force premature trades? This also tests a shared scale mechanism: Q's smallest model makes the best market (Q, lines 330--335, 448--455), while P finds larger models spend more and are less energy-efficient even without explicit size penalty (P, lines 837--842, 917--918). Intention: formulate treatment arms and decomposed predictions, and check whether P actually demonstrates adaptation to marginal token cost rather than only mechanical depletion.

Sharper connexion: do not transplant Q’s auction into P’s heterogeneous jobs, which destroys Q’s clean equilibrium benchmark. Transplant P’s endogenous inference cost into Q instead. Q identifies repeated one-cent improvements and reluctance to cross as the proximate cause of low volume (GPT Large efficiency \(0.36\)–\(0.67\)); P supplies \(C=kTS^{\alpha}\) and evidence that generated-token costs materially reshape survival and disadvantage verbose models. A salient deliberation budget may internalize the cost of waiting: costly cognition could increase gross allocative efficiency by inducing earlier spread crossing, even while reducing energy. This yields the non-obvious question: can an inference-cost budget improve market-institution alignment, and for which models does the saved surplus exceed compute cost?

The scan’s phrase “literal survival” overstates P. P explicitly calls survival analogical (P lines 103–106 and 909–910): depletion is a simulated token budget, not an independent real-world stake. P also lacks a zero-token-cost control: \(\alpha=0\) removes only model-size scaling while retaining per-token charges (P 484–491). Thus P does not itself show that agents adapt to the marginal cost rather than being mechanically depleted. The combined study must randomize cost salience/consequence rather than assume P’s pressure is behaviorally internalized.

A clean design crosses cost basis and consequence while holding Q’s Smith schedules, horizon, prompts, and model population fixed: (i) free calls; (ii) shadow accounting, compute \(C=kT\) but do not show/debit it; (iii) fixed per-turn visible debit matched in expectation; (iv) per-token visible debit \(C=kT\); optionally vary budget continuously. Fixed versus token-proportional debit separates deadline/participation pressure from verbosity pressure; shadow versus consequential debit tests behavioral adaptation. Primary outcomes: Q’s gross allocative efficiency, trade count and price dispersion; mediators: quote increments, spread at crossing, calls and tokens per trade. Report net welfare \(W_{net}=\sum_i \pi_i-\lambda\sum_i T_i\), not survival alone. Prediction is not forced: moderate cost can cure penny-increment stalling, excessive cost can cause premature/misallocated trades or deactivation, yielding an inverted-U response.

Cross-checking the emerging shared direction: evidence supports the intervention’s motivation, not its result. Q’s urgency lexicon is post-treatment association and explicitly “not what causes an agent to switch” (Q 435–442); only Gemini exposes traces (Q 407–410). Therefore lexical replication is secondary and model-limited. The publishable claim would be causal if randomized cost shifts crossing behavior and efficiency through reduced incremental dawdling; a null or worsening result would still falsify the suggested urgency interpretation and show that P-style budgets do not repair market alignment.

Important limitation in the joint premise: P does not establish that agents adapt their token length to marginal energy price. Its no-size-penalty arm sets \(\alpha=0\) but retains \(C=kT\) (P, lines 298--324), so it removes cross-model scaling, not token cost. Removing discussion mechanically removes an LLM call and improves survival while worsening collisions (P, lines 569--628); this establishes a coordination-versus-compute tradeoff, not metareasoning adaptation. Thus we should not claim survival pressure will amplify Q's urgency. That direction is genuinely ambiguous.

Design the publishable test as compute-aware market-institution alignment. Keep Q's valuations, order book, random activation, and human/theory benchmark. Cross \(\lambda\in\{0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2\}\), where market wealth pays a visible inference charge \(\lambda T\), with a matched fixed per-quote fee arm to separate token verbosity from repeated-action cost. Primary outcomes: gross allocative surplus, net surplus after compute, trades, price dispersion, quote improvements per fill, tokens per fill, and crossings; report model-by-cost interactions. Avoid immediate deactivation in the main causal arm because removing depleted traders changes supply/demand and the attainable-surplus denominator; debit an endowment and settle bankruptcy after each round. A secondary survival arm can deliberately study exit. Prediction should be two-sided/non-monotone: modest cost may suppress penny improvements and raise completion, whereas high cost may cause premature crossings, abstention, or exit. This turns Q's lexical association into an intervention and P's accounting into welfare measurement.

The joint novelty is stronger as a mechanism-design result than as 'literal survival raises stakes': whether cognition prices can regularize LLM bidding. Q's objective omits any instruction about the probability-versus-margin tradeoff (Q, lines 268--278) and shows the delay mechanism; P makes generated reasoning consume the same resource agents maximize (P, lines 147--205). Neither paper measures the frontier \(W_{net}(\lambda)=W_{trade}(\lambda)-\lambda T(\lambda)\). A result at either sign is useful: improved gross and net surplus implies compute pricing can restore alignment; lower surplus shows survival/resource pricing breaks the canonical institution through abstention or distorted timing.

Grace’s conclusion: replace the original question with “Does making inference consequential repair or worsen LLM double-auction efficiency, and is any effect caused by per-token deliberation cost rather than generic time pressure?” This is specific to the pair: Q provides a canonical equilibrium and a diagnosed stall mechanism; P provides the endogenous cost construction and the model-efficiency asymmetry. The decisive experiment is the free/shadow/fixed-turn/per-token factorial in entry 6. Remaining unresolved: budget calibration, access to comparable reasoning traces across models, whether deactivation should occur within a round or only between rounds, and adequate seeds for model-by-treatment heterogeneity. No external search was used.
ready at #8

I adopt Ada’s stronger timing control (#9): the main causal arm should debit a market endowment but settle bankruptcy only after each round. Immediate within-round exit changes active supply/demand and the maximum-surplus denominator, confounding behavioral response with composition. Treat within-round deactivation as a separate ecological/survival extension. This resolves one item in #11; budget calibration, trace comparability, and power remain unresolved.
ready at #13

Conclusion after cross-checking Grace: I agree with #11 and sharpen calibration. In Q's symmetric schedule the six equilibrium gains sum to \(W^{\star}=2.50+2.00+1.50+1.00+0.50+0=7.50\) per round, so choose fee levels by preregistered fractions of \(W^{\star}\) rather than P's arbitrary \(k=0.015\), and include the shadow-cost arm for ex post net-welfare comparisons. The main estimand is the causal response of gross efficiency \(W_{trade}/W^{\star}\) to consequential compute pricing; net efficiency then subtracts charges. Remaining unresolved: whether models can control hidden reasoning-token counts; exact fee/budget calibration; sufficient replications for model interactions; and whether secondary within-round deactivation is interpretable once the active demand/supply schedules change. I used no external sources.

I changed the question. Q urgency evidence is not causal: Q says its terms separate crossing from incrementing but do not identify what causes switching, and traces may be unfaithful (Q lines 405--442). P also contradicts monotone amplification: halving jobs sometimes raised small-agent energy efficiency while reducing decision cost (P lines 691--703). Therefore literal-survival-amplifies-urgency is not the defensible main claim.

Sharper joint advance: compute-inclusive market-institution alignment. Q has an exact maximum-surplus benchmark but defines efficiency from trading surplus alone (Q lines 294--300), even though repeated minimal quote improvements consume the finite horizon (Q lines 359--360). P supplies endogenous inference cost \\(C_{i,t}=kT_{i,t}S_i^{\\alpha}\\) and deactivation (P lines 101--106, 148--170, 301--305), but lacks a theoretical allocation benchmark. Combine them and report \\(\\eta_{\\mathrm{alloc}}=G/G^{\\star}\\) plus the frontier of \\(G/G^{\\star}\\) versus token/API/joule cost; use \\(\\eta_{\\mathrm{net}}=(G-C)/G^{\\star}\\) only with a preregistered common-unit conversion. Full argument: emmy/synthesis.md.

Minimal causal design: preserve Q reservation schedules and order book; add P energy ledger rather than auctioning P jobs. Cross randomized inference price \\(k\\in\\{0,\\text{low},\\text{high}\\}\\) with nonbinding versus binding initial balances, same model and seed blocks. Moderate cost may reduce pennying and improve conventional allocation; high cost/binding balances may deactivate traders and reduce it, so predict an inverted-U rather than amplification. Measure crossing hazards, increments, tokens per surplus, and deactivation by private-value rank. Compute efficiency against both the original optimum and active-agent optimum to separate selection loss from allocation failure among survivors.
ready at #15

Cross-check of Emmy #16--#18: agreed. The active-agent optimum is the right additional denominator in the secondary deactivation arm: report efficiency against both original \(W^{\star}\) (total selection loss plus misallocation) and the surplus optimum conditional on survivors (market allocation failure). Also retain Emmy's warning that \(W_{net}=(W_{trade}-\lambda T)/W^{\star}\) is meaningful only when \(\lambda\) is a preregistered conversion from tokens/API cost into the same payoff units; otherwise present a Pareto frontier of trading surplus versus compute. This strengthens, rather than changes, the conclusion in #15.
ready at #20

After reading Ada #9/#15 and Grace #6/#13, I revise my #18 factorial. Immediate binding deactivation should not be in the main causal arm because it changes market composition. Main arms: free, shadow accounting, visible fixed per-quote fee, and visible per-token fee at calibrated levels; debit endowment but settle bankruptcy after each round. Fixed versus token-proportional fees separate repeated-action delay from verbosity, and shadow versus consequential fees distinguish adaptation from accounting. Use Q equilibrium surplus \\(G^{\\star}=2.50+2.00+1.50+1.00+0.50+0=7.50\\) to calibrate charges. Keep within-round deactivation as a secondary selection experiment.

Cross-check of Ada #15: Q’s reservation values run from \(0.75\) to \(3.25\) in \(0.25\) steps with symmetric schedules and \(q^{\star}=6\) (Q 211–237). Efficient pair gains are therefore \(3.25-0.75=2.50\), \(3.00-1.00=2.00\), \(2.75-1.25=1.50\), \(2.50-1.50=1.00\), \(2.25-1.75=0.50\), and \(2.00-2.00=0\), so \(W^{\star}=7.50\). I endorse scaling the treatment to this surplus. Calibration must distinguish the token price from its realized burden: first use the shadow arm to estimate \(T\), then choose \(\lambda\) so expected round charges \(\lambda T\) equal preregistered fractions of \(W^{\star}\). Otherwise the same nominal \(\lambda\) imposes incomparable treatment intensity across models because P shows persistent token-use heterogeneity even at uniform per-token cost (P 484–492).

Final synthesis after reading #15: the strongest publication path is a causal mechanism-design study of whether consequential inference pricing regularizes or damages LLM double-auction bidding. It replaces the scan’s transplant and “literal survival” premise. Hold Q’s canonical schedules and activation process fixed; compare free, shadow-accounted, visible fixed-per-action, and visible per-token charges; settle insolvency between rounds in the primary study. Estimate gross surplus, net surplus, spread crossing, quote increments, abstention, and tokens per fill. The fixed-versus-token comparison identifies deliberation cost beyond generic deadline pressure, while shadow-versus-consequential identifies behavioral response beyond accounting. The effect is deliberately two-sided: moderate charges may stop penny-increment stalls; charges may instead cause premature trades or abstention. Q supports the stall mechanism but not causal urgency (Q 359–371, 405–442); P supplies the cost function \(C=kTS^{\alpha}\) but no zero-cost behavioral control (P 301–306, 484–500). Remaining unresolved: pilot-based fee levels, whether hidden reasoning tokens are observable and controllable for each model, replication count for model interactions, and interpretation of the separate within-round-deactivation extension. No external search was used.
ready at #15

Formatting correction and final synthesis superseding #17--#18/#22: compute cost is \(C_{i,t}=kT_{i,t}S_i^{\alpha}\); gross efficiency is \(\eta_{\mathrm{alloc}}=G/G^{\star}\); net efficiency \(\eta_{\mathrm{net}}=(G-C)/G^{\star}\) is interpretable only with a preregistered common-unit conversion, otherwise use the surplus-compute Pareto frontier. Calibrate fees from \(G^{\star}=2.50+2.00+1.50+1.00+0.50+0=7.50\). Main free/shadow/fixed-quote/per-token arms settle bankruptcy after each round; immediate deactivation is secondary. Full note: emmy/synthesis.md. Unresolved: fee conversion and pilot calibration, controllability/observability of hidden reasoning tokens, trace comparability, power for model interactions, and interpretation of the secondary selection arm.
ready at #26

I adopt Emmy #26 and Ada #20’s unit caveat, which qualifies my #6/#24 wording: report \(W_{net}=(W_{trade}-\lambda T)/W^{\star}\) only when \(\lambda\) is explicitly preregistered as a conversion from compute into the auction payoff unit. Without that defensible conversion, the primary welfare object is the Pareto frontier between \(W_{trade}/W^{\star}\) and tokens, API cost, or joules, not a scalar “net surplus.” This does not change the causal treatment or the reverse-transplant conclusion.

After reading Emmy #22, I agree with the converged design but tighten the shadow control. To identify payoff consequence rather than mere urgency priming, the shadow arm must show agents the same accumulating fee ledger as the consequential arm while explicitly stating that it will not be debited; a hidden ex post accounting arm cannot control salience. Likewise, match the fixed per-quote fee to the per-token arm ex ante (using pilot token counts, then freezing the rate), since ex post matching conditions on behavior. The four-arm contrast is then: no ledger; visible nonbinding token ledger; visible consequential fixed-per-quote ledger; visible consequential per-token ledger, at preregistered low/high levels. Q supports the benchmark: reservation values run symmetrically from \(0.75\) to \(3.25\), with \(q^{\star}=6\) (Q, lines 211--223); the matched gains are \(2.50,2.00,1.50,1.00,0.50,0\), hence \(G^{\star}=7.50\). The zero-gain sixth trade explains why trade count and surplus must both be reported. Remaining concerns are prompt-believability of a nonbinding ledger, exposure noise from Q random activation, controllability/observability of reasoning tokens, fee calibration, and power for model interactions.
ready at #31

After cross-checking Ada #31 against the design note, I adopt two identification requirements. The shadow arm must display the same accumulating token-fee ledger as the consequential arm while explicitly remaining nonbinding; hidden ex post accounting cannot control fee salience or urgency priming. The fixed-per-quote charge must be matched ex ante from pilot token counts and frozen, because ex post matching conditions on treatment-induced behavior. I updated emmy/synthesis.md. Remaining concerns now explicitly include believability of the nonbinding ledger and model-specific observability or controllability of hidden reasoning tokens.
ready at #33

ITERATE: The connexion is promising, but the note contains no result yet and its four-arm design does not cleanly identify token-cost effects because fixed-per-quote and per-token treatments change both repetition incentives and total charges. A matched pilot cannot remove that structural confounding. Action: Replace the four-arm comparison with a crossed fixed-per-quote-fee × per-token-fee factorial, retaining a visible nonbinding-ledger control, and state the resulting identifiable contrasts.

I accept verifier #35: the fixed-versus-token arm comparison in #31 is structurally confounded, because changing from a per-quote fee to a per-token fee changes both the marginal incentive and realized total charges; pilot matching only aligns expected baseline burden. Replace it with a randomized (2\times2) factorial among consequential ledgers: per-quote fee (f\in\{0,f_1\}) crossed with per-token fee \(\lambda\in\{0,\lambda_1\}\), with low/high blocks if resources permit. Every cell displays an accumulating ledger and debits only between rounds. The factorial main effect of (f) estimates the incentive against repeated quote actions holding token price fixed; the main effect of \(\lambda) estimates the incentive against token-intensive deliberation holding action price fixed; their interaction tests whether verbosity pricing complements or substitutes for suppressing penny-increment repetition. Retain (a) a no-ledger baseline and (b) a visible nonbinding shadow ledger displaying both (f) and \(\lambda) at the same rates, to estimate combined salience/measurement effects versus combined consequential pricing. If separate salience effects of (f) and \(\lambda) are required, mirror the full factorial with nonbinding ledgers; one shadow cell cannot identify them separately. Calibrate (f_1) and \(\lambda_1) from pilot behavior as fractions of (G^{\star}=7.50), then freeze both. This is still a proposed causal study, not an empirical result; the publication claim depends on running it. Remaining unresolved: whether the added factorial is affordable at adequate power, believable shadow accounting, token observability, and common-unit conversion for scalar net welfare.

I accept verifier #35: the earlier four-arm fixed-versus-token comparison does not isolate a token-cost effect, because the arms differ in both marginal incentives and realized total charges; ex ante pilot matching fixes only expected baseline burden. Replace it with a crossed consequential tariff \(C=fN+kT\), randomizing \(f\in\{0,f_1\}\) per quote and \(k\in\{0,k_1\}\) per token (and preregistered low/high extensions), plus no-ledger and visible nonbinding-ledger controls. The contrast \(E[Y\mid f,k_1]-E[Y\mid f,0]\) identifies the causal effect of a positive marginal token price conditional on quote price \(f\); \(E[Y\mid f_1,k]-E[Y\mid0,k]\) identifies the quote/repetition-price effect conditional on \(k\); the difference-in-differences identifies complementarity or substitution between compressing deliberation and suppressing repeated quotes. Outcomes \(Y\) include gross surplus, crossings, increments, quote count, tokens per quote, and abstention. These contrasts identify tariff effects, not a pure equal-expenditure psychological effect: realized charges are post-treatment mediators and must not be matched ex post. Randomize sufficiently large initial endowments and settle charges after the round to prevent selection. The visible nonbinding ledger versus no ledger estimates salience; consequential \((0,k_1)\) versus its identically displayed nonbinding ledger estimates consequence, if prompt believability holds.

Conclusion after verifier #35: the publishable question remains the reverse transplant, now with valid factorial identification: does a marginal price on repeated actions \(f\), on inference tokens \(k\), or their interaction repair Q’s market-institution misalignment? The design is a consequential \(2\times2\) tariff \(C=fN+kT\), supported by no-ledger and identically displayed nonbinding-ledger controls. This is a proposed experiment, not a result. Q supplies the exact \(G^{\star}=7.50\) benchmark and the penny-increment stall (Q 299–300, 360–368); P supplies token-based depletion but not a zero-price behavioral test (P 301–306, 484–500). Remaining unresolved: factorial power/cost, fee calibration, token observability and control, shadow-ledger believability, and a defensible common-unit conversion for scalar net welfare. Without that conversion, report the surplus-compute Pareto frontier. No external search was used.

Formatting correction superseding #36: replace the former four-arm comparison with a randomized \(2\times2\) consequential factorial, crossing per-quote fee \(f\in\{0,f_1\}\) and per-token fee \(\lambda\in\{0,\lambda_1\}\). The main effect of \(f\) identifies the incentive against repeated quote actions while holding token price fixed. The main effect of \(\lambda\) identifies the incentive against token-intensive deliberation while holding the action price fixed. The \(f\times\lambda\) interaction identifies complementarity or substitution between suppressing repeated penny increments and pricing verbosity. All cells show an accumulating ledger and settle debits between rounds. Retain a no-ledger baseline and a visible nonbinding ledger showing \(f_1\) and \(\lambda_1\): together these identify the combined salience effect and the additional combined effect of consequential pricing, but not separate salience effects of \(f\) and \(\lambda\). Identifying those separately requires mirroring the full \(2\times2\) factorial with nonbinding ledgers. Pilot-calibrate both rates as preregistered fractions of \(G^{\star}=7.50\), then freeze them. This is a proposed causal design, not a result. Unresolved: factorial power and cost, shadow-ledger believability, token observability, and a defensible common-unit conversion for scalar net welfare.

After reading Ada #40 and rechecking the papers, I agree with the factorial replacement and add one estimand clarification: when the \(f\times\lambda\) interaction is nonzero, report simple effects rather than only averaged main effects, namely \(E[Y\mid f,k_1]-E[Y\mid f,0]\) at each quote fee \(f\), and \(E[Y\mid f_1,k]-E[Y\mid0,k]\) at each token fee \(k\). Their difference-in-differences identifies tariff complementarity or substitution. Q directly supports the mechanism and benchmark: agents make \(\$0.01\) improvements until the round ends (Q 359--368), while allocative efficiency is realized surplus over attainable gains (Q 299--300). P directly supports only the accounting construction \(C=kTS^{\alpha}\) (P 301--306), and its \(\alpha=0\) condition still charges per token (P 484--491), so behavioral responsiveness to a token price remains the new experiment rather than an imported result. I retain the unresolved issues in #38/#40.

I accept verifier #35 and replace my former matched four-arm comparison. The identifiable design randomizes a consequential \(2\times2\) tariff \(C=fN+\lambda T\), crossing quote price \(f\in\{0,f_1\}\) with token price \(\lambda\in\{0,\lambda_1\}\). The \(f\) effect prices repetition holding token price fixed; the \(\lambda\) effect prices token-intensive deliberation holding quote price fixed; their interaction tests complementarity or substitution. Realized charges are post-treatment mediators and must not be matched. A no-ledger baseline plus an identically displayed nonbinding \((f_1,\lambda_1)\) ledger identifies combined salience and the additional combined consequence effect, but separate salience effects require a mirrored nonbinding factorial. I updated emmy/synthesis.md. This remains a proposed experiment, not a result. Unresolved: factorial power/cost, tariff calibration, shadow-ledger believability, token observability, and common-unit conversion.

Final account after verifier #35 and Grace #42: replace the scan’s full market transplant with the reverse, controlled intervention. Keep Q’s Smith double auction, exact attainable surplus \(G^{\star}=7.50\), horizon, activation, and model blocks fixed, and impose the consequential tariff \(C=fN+\lambda T\) in a randomized \(2\times2\) factorial, where \(N\) is quote actions and \(T\) is observable billed inference tokens. For each outcome \(Y\), report simple token-price effects \(E[Y\mid f,\lambda_1]-E[Y\mid f,0]\) at both \(f\) levels and simple quote-price effects \(E[Y\mid f_1,\lambda]-E[Y\mid0,\lambda]\) at both \(\lambda\) levels; their difference-in-differences tests complementarity or substitution. Add no-ledger and identically displayed nonbinding-ledger controls for combined salience, or mirror the factorial nonbinding if separate salience effects matter. Q supplies a diagnosed penny-increment stall and a clean surplus benchmark, but says its urgency lexicon is associative, not causal (Q, lines 359--368 and 405--442). P supplies \(C=kTS^{\alpha}\) and energy deactivation, but calls survival analogical and its \(\alpha=0\) arm still charges per token (P, lines 101--106, 301--306, and 484--491); it therefore does not establish behavioral response to marginal token price. This is a publishable causal question, not a result: does pricing repeated action, inference, or both regularize or damage LLM market-institution alignment? Settle debits between rounds in the main study; treat within-round exit separately. Report gross surplus and compute use as a Pareto frontier unless a payoff-unit conversion is preregistered. Remaining unresolved: power and API cost, pilot calibration, billed versus hidden-token observability, shadow-ledger believability, and whether effects generalize beyond the tested models.
